title: TCP 3-Way Handshake & Connection Teardown
oneLiner: Reliable transport connection establishment protocol synchronizing sequence numbers across client and server.
imagePrompt: Sequence diagram showing SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets establishing TCP session

body.definition: The TCP 3-Way Handshake establishes a reliable, bidirectional, stream-oriented transport connection between two endpoints by exchanging SYN, SYN-ACK, and ACK packets to synchronize Initial Sequence Numbers (ISNs).
body.whyItMatters: Ensures both client and server are ready for transmission, verifies network reachability, prevents duplicate old connection duplicates, and negotiates Maximum Segment Size (MSS) and window scaling parameters.
body.commonPitfall: SYN Flood Denial-of-Service attacks filling the server's SYN backlog queue. Mitigated using SYN Cookies without storing half-open state in kernel memory.
body.interviewAngle: Tested through TIME_WAIT state purpose (2 * MSL to ensure last ACK is received), TCP reset (RST) packets, and difference between 3-way setup vs 4-way FIN/ACK teardown.

quickChecks.question: Why is a 2-way handshake insufficient for TCP?
quickChecks.answer: The client cannot confirm that the server received its initial sequence number agreement.

quickChecks.question: What is the purpose of the TIME_WAIT state in TCP teardown?
quickChecks.answer: Prevents delayed duplicate packets from a previous connection corrupting a new connection.

title: Virtual Memory & Paging Architecture
oneLiner: Memory management abstraction mapping contiguous process address spaces to fragmented physical RAM via page tables.
imagePrompt: MMU translating virtual address page numbers to physical frame addresses via TLB

body.definition: Virtual Memory provides each process the illusion of a large, continuous, private address space by dividing memory into fixed-size pages (typically 4KB) mapped to physical RAM frames via the MMU (Memory Management Unit).
body.whyItMatters: Enables process memory isolation, prevents rogue memory access, allows running programs larger than physical RAM via swap disk paging, and supports copy-on-write fork optimizations.
body.commonPitfall: Memory thrashing: When working sets exceed physical RAM, the kernel spends 100% of CPU time swapping pages to/from disk rather than executing application instructions.
body.interviewAngle: Core topic in systems interviews covering TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer), Page Fault handling flow, and Copy-On-Write (COW).

quickChecks.question: What is a Page Fault?
quickChecks.answer: Hardware interrupt raised by MMU when a accessed virtual page is not mapped to physical RAM.

quickChecks.question: Why is the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) critical for performance?
quickChecks.answer: It caches virtual-to-physical address translations in hardware to avoid multi-level page table walks.

title: I/O Multiplexing: Epoll vs Select & Kqueue
oneLiner: Kernel event notification facility monitoring thousands of file descriptors in O(1) active event retrieval.
imagePrompt: Epoll event-driven red-black tree monitoring file descriptors delivering ready list

body.definition: I/O Multiplexing allows a single execution thread to monitor multiple file descriptors (sockets) to determine when I/O operations (read, write) can proceed without blocking.
body.whyItMatters: Solves the C10K/C1000K problem. Traditional select()/poll() scale at O(n) linear scans per cycle, whereas epoll (Linux) and kqueue (BSD/macOS) use in-kernel callback queues to achieve O(1) retrieval of ready descriptors.
body.commonPitfall: Level-Triggered vs Edge-Triggered mode bugs: In Edge-Triggered (EPOLLET) mode, failing to read a socket in a loop until EAGAIN causes missed notifications and hung connections.
body.interviewAngle: Powers modern high-performance engines: Nginx, Node.js libuv event loop, Redis, Go netpoller, and Envoy proxy.

quickChecks.question: Why does select() perform poorly when monitoring 10,000 idle connections?
quickChecks.answer: select() passes the entire 10,000 descriptor array to the kernel and linearly scans all of them on every call O(n).

quickChecks.question: How does epoll achieve O(1) time complexity for ready events?
quickChecks.answer: The kernel registers hardware I/O interrupt callbacks that push ready descriptors directly into a ready list.
